newsitem.title: USA: Fruit fly pheromones give clues to sex appeal.
newsitem.headline: Fruit fly pheromones give clues to sex appeal.

text.p: The nature of sexual attraction -- homosexual as well as heterosexual -- is far more complex than previously believed, even in such simple creatures as fruit flies, scientists report.

"The complex nature of sexual identity in an animal as relatively simple as the fruit fly indicates that simplistic explanations of the genetic bases of sexuality are unlikely to be true," researchers wrote in an article to be published in Friday's edition of the journal Science.
By manipulating fruit fly pheromones, the chemical signals that elicit sexual responses, researchers found that male flies who got feminine pheromones drew attention from other males.

However, these so-called "perfumed" male flies did not necessarily return the homosexual attention, according to Jean-Francois Ferveur of the Universite Paris-Sud at Orsay, France, one of the article's authors.
"The feminized male is still able to show a heterosexual orientation: he is not confused or autostimulated by his own feminine perfume," Ferveur told Reuters via e-mail.
In fruit flies, homosexual attraction can occur if only one male has feminized pheromones, which send out a "come hither" signal inviting male courtship, Ferveur and his co-authors found.

Building on an earlier study that feminized male fruit flies' neurons, these findings show that there are at least two ways to genetically induce homosexual behaviour, Ferveur said: "either by feminizing the brain of the courter, or the pheromones of the courtee."
However, he said that there was no direct relation between these two observations, suggesting that "the very simplistic and reductionist explanation concerning the genetics or sexuality are wrong."

Even in insects, research has shown that there are various levels determining sexual orientation. For humans, whose sex appeal is also governed in part by pheromones, the answer is likely to be still more complex and difficult to pinpoint, Ferveur said.

"... (T)here a more determinants that built the sexual orientation of humans," he said. Other variables besides pheromones could include whether human sexual orientation remains constant during life. Other factors might take in societal and historical influences, Ferveur said.
